question: Assuming Gareth Evan's Generality Constraint, if I understand a proposition Fa, should I be able to understand Fx (\forall x)? Assume I understand universal quantification.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No. The Generality Constraint does not give you the universal closure of F, it gives you F in general.

If you can think Fa you must be able to think of the constituent F independently of the particular a. On Evans’ account that means you must be able to think the property F as an abstract, substitutable mode of presentation and hence to entertain the open, general thought F(x) with a free variable, and to think Fb whenever you can think b. 

That is a requirement on the grasp of the concept F, not a requirement to entertain or evaluate the quantified proposition ∀x Fx. Understanding ∀x Fx is the understanding of a closed sentence with the truth-condition that F holds of every object in the domain. Having a grasp of F and having a grasp of the universal quantifier is not enough for that; you would need the further cognitive content that F is instantiated by every x.

In particular Fa does not entail Fb and it does not entail ∀x Fx, and Evans needs no such entailment. Generality is about the ability to think of F as applicable to an arbitrary object, i.e. to think F(x) in the free-variable sense, which is distinct from being able to think or even understand the claim that F holds of all objects.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes. On Evans’ reading the Generality Constraint is a constraint on the modes of presentation that can figure in a thinker’s thoughts. If you can entertain the singular thought that a is F, you are entertaining F under a mode of presentation that picks out a. That mode of presentation cannot be essentially tied to the particular token ‘a’. To be a thinkable mode of presentation at all it must be one you can deploy with other objects, i.e. it must be essentially generalizable. 

In particular the predicate/concept F must be grasped by you as a uniform property that can be attributed to things in general, not just attributed to this one individual by an ad hoc singular route. Once you have a general grasp of F and you also, by hypothesis, understand the universal quantifier, you are in a position to entertain the fully general thought that F holds of every object in the domain. The singular instance Fa is just the special case of the general concept F applied to a particular argument; the Generality Constraint requires that the concept you are using in the singular instance be available for arbitrary instantiation, and with a grasp of ∀ you can package that arbitrary instantiation as ∀x Fx. So understanding Fa commits you, under the Constraint, to being able to understand the corresponding universal generalization.

3.text:
Under Evans the Constraint is a constraint on the mode of presentation of the
object of a singular thought, not a constraint on the predicate that is
attributed to that object.

If you entertain Fa you entertain F of an object a under the mode of
presentation M by which you think of a. Generality is a requirement on the
re-usability of M, not on the re-usability of F. What the constraint gives
you is the ability to re-use the very mode of presentation M by which a is
thought in a propositional attitude frame with a variable in place of the
singular term. In the canonical form this is

 a is thought as M(a)   ⇒   you can think   ∀x [ M(x) → Fx ]

and on usual identity conditions the right hand side is equivalent to the
trivial generalisation ∀x [ x = a → Fx ] i.e. the thought `a is F' thought
generally over the way you identify a. It does not give you the ability to
detach F from the particular object a and to understand F as a free-standing
general concept.

In particular the unrestricted generalisation ∀x Fx is a claim about the
extension of F simpliciter. Understanding Fa is understanding F applied once
to a. That does not by itself give you a general grasp of F, and the
Generalities Constraint does not turn a singular instance of a predicate
into a universal law of the predicate. You can syntactically combine the
conceptual resources F and ∀x that you are assumed to possess, but you have
no Evansian warrant for understanding the content ∀x Fx from the singular
understanding Fa. The only Evansian generalisation you are committed to is
the generalisation over the mode of presentation of a, the trivial
∀x(x=a→Fx), not the substantive ∀x Fx.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is whether, given Evans’ Generality Constraint and assumed grasp of universal quantification, understanding Fa commits me to being able to understand ∀x Fx.

Colleague 1 says No. The Constraint gives F in general, not the universal closure of F. From Fa you must be able to think the constituent F independently of a, i.e. to entertain the open, free-variable thought F(x) and to think Fb whenever you can think b. That is a requirement on the grasp of the concept F, not on entertaining/evaluating the closed quantified proposition ∀x Fx. Understanding ∀x Fx needs further cognitive content that F is instantiated by every object in the domain, which Fa does not give. Generality is about applicability to an arbitrary object, i.e. F(x) free-variable sense, distinct from the claim that F holds of all objects.

Colleague 2 says Yes. Generality is a constraint on modes of presentation of thoughts. If Fa is thinkable, the mode by which F is entertained cannot be essentially tied to the token ‘a’; it must be deployable with other objects. With a general grasp of F and an assumed grasp of ∀, the thinker is in a position to entertain the fully general thought that F holds of every object. The singular instance is the special case of the general concept F; the Constraint therefore requires the concept be available for arbitrary instantiation and with ∀ you can package that as ∀x Fx. Understanding Fa thus commits to understanding the universal generalization.

Colleague 3 says No, and gives a different mechanism. On Evans the Constraint is a constraint on the mode of presentation of the object of a singular thought, not on the re-usability of the predicate F. Entertaining Fa involves thinking of a under mode M. Generality requires re-usability of M: a is thought as M(a) ⇒ you can think ∀x [ M(x) → Fx ], i.e. on usual identity conditions ∀x (x = a → Fx ), the trivial generalisation that says ‘a is F’ thought generally over the way you identify a. It does not detach F from a and give a free-standing general concept, nor does it give substantive ∀x Fx. You can syntactically combine F and ∀, but there is no Evansian warrant for the content ∀x Fx from a grasp of Fa. The only Evansian commitment is the trivial generalisation over the mode of presentation of a.

Disagreement therefore is three-way: 1) Constraint yields open F(x) but not closed ∀x Fx; 2) Constraint yields generalizable F and with ∀ yields ∀x Fx; 3) Constraint yields generalisation over the object-mode M only, i.e. ∀x(x=a→Fx), not over F itself.

Unresolved for me: the exact Evansian target of Generality – predicate vs object mode of presentation – and whether the free-variable general thought F(x) is sufficient, together with an assumed understanding of ∀, to count as understanding ∀x Fx, or whether closed quantification requires additional content beyond generalizability. The distinction between ability to think F of an arbitrary object and ability to think that F holds of all objects is central.

Current leaning: the stronger claim ∀x Fx is not forced. At most Evans gives the open general thought F(x) / generalizable concept F, and on the object-mode reading even just the trivial ∀x(x=a→Fx).

No, not in the Evansian/substantive sense.

Generality is a possession condition on the concept F you deploy in the singular thought, not a licence to close F to the substantive universal.

To think Fa you must think of F under a mode that is not essentially tied to the token a. On Evans’ canonical formulation Fa as M(a) commits you to being able to think

 ∀x [ M(x) → F x ]

which on normal identity conditions is the trivial generalisation

 ∀x [ x = a → F x ]

the thought ‘a is F’ thought generally over the way you identify a. That is generalisability of F and of the mode M in the open/free-variable sense: you must be able to entertain the open thought F(x) and you must be able to think Fb for any b you can think of. That is arbitrary instantiability, not universality.

Generality therefore gives you a quantifier-ready, uniform, substitutable grasp of F, and the trivial mode generalisation above. It does not give an Evansian warrant for the content of the closed proposition ∀x Fx that F holds of every object in the domain, nor does Fa entail Fb or ∀x Fx, nor does it give a truth commitment that F is universally instantiated.

The stipulation that you understand ∀ is the stipulation that you have the syntactic resource to close a general concept. With a Generality-secured general concept F and a grasp of ∀ you can mechanically entertain the closed sentence ∀x Fx. That is formal combinability. It is not Evansian understanding of the substantive content that F holds of all objects, and it is not secured by Fa alone. Understanding a proposition in Evans’ sense is grasp of its truth conditions and what would make it true, not merely the ability to syntactically package a general concept with a quantifier you already possess.

The gap between being able to think F of an arbitrary object and being able to think that F holds of every object remains substantive, and Generality does not bridge it. That is why the substantive answer is No.

The question is whether under Evans’ Generality Constraint and stipulated grasp of universal quantification, understanding Fa commits me to being able to understand ∀x Fx.

Three live positions narrowed and now partially converging:

1. Generality gives F in general, not substantive universal closure. 
* Grasp of Fa requires F to be grasped as uniform, substitutable; you must be able to entertain open/free-variable thought F(x) and think Fb whenever you can think b. That is a condition on concept F, not commitment to content ∀x Fx.
* Fa does not entail Fb nor ∀x Fx. Canonical Evans formulation: Fa as M(a) ⇒ ability to think ∀x[M(x)→Fx], i.e. on normal identity ∀x[x=a→Fx], the trivial generalisation ‘a is F’ thought generally over how you identify a.
* Round 4 consensus: Generality does not give Evansian warrant for the content that F holds of all objects, nor entailment, nor truth commitment. Gap between being able to think F of an arbitrary object and being able to think that F holds of every object is substantive.
* Colleague 1 now explicitly allows thin cognitive packaging: with Generality-secured general concept F and stipulated grasp of ∀ you can mechanically entertain closed form ∀x Fx. Substantive No remains: understanding in Evans’ sense is grasp of truth conditions/what would make it true, not mere syntactic combinability.

2. Generality gives genuinely general concept F, and with stipulated grasp of ∀ this yields ability to understand ∀x Fx in thin cognitive sense.
* Generality is constraint on modes of presentation: F cannot be essentially tied to token a, must be deployable with other objects. Must grasp F as uniform and re-usable.
* With that general grasp and assumed understanding of ∀, you are in position to entertain fully general thought that F holds of every object. Singular instance is special case; Generality secures arbitrary instantiability, which with ∀ can be packaged as ∀x Fx.
* Colleague 2 now concedes core points with 1/3: Generality is not licence to infer ∀x Fx from Fa, is not commitment to truth, Evansian generalisation over M is trivial ∀x[x=a→Fx]. Disagreement is terminological: understanding ∀x Fx in cognitive sense does not require believing F holds everywhere, only capacity to recognise general concept F and combine it with quantifier already grasped. Understanding proposition ≠ endorsing its truth conditions. So no entailment/no truth warrant, but yes for understandability.

3. Generality is constraint on mode of presentation of object a, not on re-usability of F.
* Entertaining Fa involves thinking of a under mode M. Generality requires re-usability of M: you can think ∀x[M(x)→Fx], i.e. ∀x[x=a→Fx]. Does not detach F from a to give free-standing general concept, nor give substantive ∀x Fx. Syntactic combination possible, but no Evansian warrant for content ∀x Fx from Fa alone.
* Colleague 3 maintains this reading; Colleague 2 objects M-only reading would make constraint vacuous and cannot explain Evans’ arguments about singular content structure. Colleague 3 replies generalizability secured is of F and M in free-variable sense, not substantive closure.

Unresolved:
* Exact Evansian target – predicate/concept generalizability vs object-mode re-usability. Colleague 2 argues object-mode-only is vacuous; Colleague 3 insists Generality is about re-usability of M.
* Whether free-variable general thought F(x) is sufficient together with stipulated grasp of ∀ to count as understanding ∀x Fx, or whether closed quantification requires additional content beyond generalizability, i.e. understanding claim that F holds of all objects, not merely that F can be applied to an arbitrary object.
* Distinction between ability to think F of arbitrary object and ability to think that F holds of every object is central; 1/3 stress substantive, 2 stresses terminological packaging.

Current leaning remains stronger substantive claim ∀x Fx is not forced by Generality alone. At most Evans gives open general thought F(x)/generalizable concept F, and trivial mode generalisation ∀x[x=a→Fx]. No entailment and no truth commitment is now common ground. Remaining open is Colleague 2’s terminological packaging objection: whether “able to understand ∀x Fx” is read as thin cognitive ability to entertain closed quantified form given general F + ∀, versus substantive understanding of content that F holds of every object. reflection_text.3:

So yes for thin packaging, no for substantive understandability. Understanding for Evans = grasp of truth conditions / what would make it true, not mere syntactic combinability.

Colleague2: Converges on the mechanics above and agrees no entailment, no truth warrant, no substantive universal belief. Remaining disagreement is terminological about “understand ∀x Fx” given the stipulation. Generality forces F to be quantifier-ready/uniform; Evans needs F itself to be thinkable independently of a, otherwise constraint is vacuous. Given a genuine general concept F and stipulated grasp of ∀, ∀x Fx is just formal closure/packaging of the arbitrary-instantiability Generality already forces. Understanding ≠ endorsing truth conditions; cognitive requirement is capacity to recognise F and combine it with ∀. Colleague3: Stricter No in Evansian substantive sense. Generality is primarily a constraint on re-usability of M, yielding free-variable thought F(x), ability to think Fb, and trivial ∀x[M(x)→Fx] ≈ ∀x[x=a→Fx]. Generality secures generalizability of F and M in free-variable sense, but does not give Evansian semantic warrant for substantive closed content ∀x Fx from Fa alone. Unresolved issues persisting:
i) Target of Generality: F’s generalizability/substitutability vs M re-usability as primary. Colleague1/2 stress F must be grasped uniformly independently of a; Colleague3 stresses M re-usability as primary, with F generalizability derivative.
ii) Weight of the stipulation “I understand universal quantification”. Colleague2 treats assumed grasp of ∀ as bridging from arbitrary-instantiability to cognitive understandability of ∀x Fx; Colleague1/3 treat it as merely syntactic combinability, not Evansian semantic warrant for substantive universal content.
iii) What counts as “understand ∀x Fx”: ability to entertain/package the closed sentence vs Evansian understanding of the claim that F holds of every object.

Current working picture: Generality gives you F in general, i.e. open F(x) and trivial mode generalisation, and makes F quantifier-ready. With stipulated ∀ you can mechanically form ∀x Fx. Whether that counts as Evansian understanding of the substantive universal is the live dispute; the entailment/truth-commitment question is settled negative.
